title: Insuring the breach
dek: Ransomware and identity fraud are flooding the cyber insurance market with unpredictable claims, forcing a harder underwriting line and bifurcating the risk pool.
lede: Every business now expects to be breached. That expectation spawned a $7 billion cyber liability insurance market in the US alone that's already breaking at the seams. Ransomware claims exploded in 2025, identity theft is getting weirder and more expensive, and the insurers who once priced risk by formula are now gatekeeping who gets covered at all.
what_changed:
Cyber liability insurance used to be a soft market—cheap premiums, broad coverage, happy underwriters. That era ended hard in 2025. Ransomware, which was always a risk, became the risk: it drove more than 90 percent of all cyber insurance claim value in the first half of 2025 alone. Businesses that got hit faced ransom demands that jumped 47 percent year-over-year, though to insurers' relief, 86 percent of targets refused to pay. But the claims that did land were massive. Technology companies averaged $875,000 per ransomware incident, finance and insurance hit $731,000, and healthcare $675,000. Third-party liability claims—lawsuits from customers and partners blaming your breach for their losses—surged 70 percent in a single year, the biggest jump the industry tracked. That's not a trend; that's a phase shift. By mid-2025, Beazley (one of the big players) posted a 48.5 percent loss ratio, and the sector as a whole saw the first half of 2025 rack up more claim severity than most full years prior.

The market is physically fragmenting. For the first time in years, the combined ratio tightened to 65.4 percent in 2025—which sounds good on paper (breakeven is 100 percent), but the tightness came entirely from underwriters culling risk, not from premiums rising. Two years of rate cuts have ended; S&P Global now forecasts 15 to 20 percent premium increases for 2026. But here's the brutal part: those increases won't be uniform. Businesses with strong cybersecurity posture will get cheap rates. Laggards will be denied outright or shunted to the surplus market at triple premiums. The gap between a protected firm and a vulnerable one is widening fast. California's new CCPA cybersecurity audit mandate (effective January 2026) is already driving demand for cyber insurance among tech, retail, and financial firms, but it's also raising the floor for underwriting—you either have clean audits or you don't get a desk at the table. Insurers like AIG are now running 700-plus cybersecurity variables through AI platforms just to decide whether to offer a quote. This is not boutique risk management anymore; it's a hard gate.

Identity theft insurance is seeing a different crisis: synthetic identity fraud. Real identity theft—someone steals your Social Security number and opens a credit card in your name—is common and expensive. But synthetic identity fraud, where criminals fabricate entire personas from fragments of stolen data, is now 25 percent of all fraudulent claims and jumped eightfold globally in 2025. Life insurers faced $3.3 billion in synthetic ID exposure through 2024 and saw instances explode in the following year. The claims data looks like traditional fraud (it's fraud), but the forensics are alien—there's no victim in the classic sense, just a fiction that made money before it vanished. That forces underwriters to rethink loss reserves, claims assessment, and who even bears the cost. Simultaneously, the competitive field is sorting itself by technology. Aura's dark-web monitoring catches 260 distinct signals; competitors like Norton LifeLock track 60. Aura alerts triggered in 3 minutes in Q1 2026 tests; LifeLock's came 9.2 hours later. Biometric liveness detection with AI deepfake defense is the 2026 standard—you can't sell identity protection without it anymore. Credit bureaus (Equifax, Experian, TransUnion) are bundling monitoring and insurance to lock in wallet share, and consolidators like Kingswood Capital are scooping up smaller players like IDX to stitch together breach response and insurance into one package. The industry is consolidating toward full-stack protection vendors, not bare-bones insurers.

Regulatory tightening is the third pressure. California's CCPA audit mandate took effect in January 2026, and the FTC updated identity theft rules in August 2026. The FTC's 2024 data already showed $12.5 billion in fraud losses—up 25 percent year-over-year—with identity theft now 18 percent of all Consumer Sentinel complaints. That metric alone tells you the margin for error is vanishing. Underwriters used to assume a certain baseline of fraud in the pool and price accordingly. Now they're pricing for volatility and regulatory penalty. A single class-action lawsuit over a major breach can cost millions; cyber insurers are pricing that in. Identity insurers face tighter claim standards and have to justify every denial to regulators. The whole market is shifting from loose-and-broad to tight-and-selective.

evidence: Cyber Liability Insurance: US market $7.02B in 2024 (19.3% CAGR through 2026), North America $9.56B in 2025; ransomware drove 90%+ of claim severity in H1 2025.

Technology: Highest average ransomware severity at $875,000 per incident in 2025; AIG deployed AI underwriting screening 700+ cybersecurity variables per policy in late 2025.
Healthcare: Ransomware claims average $675,000; third-party liability surged 70% YoY, forcing hospitals and health systems to face lawsuits from patients over breach damages.
Identity Theft Insurance: $6.8B market in 2024 growing 8–15% CAGR through 2035; synthetic identity fraud (25% of claims, 8x growth in 2025) forces rethinking of loss reserves and claim assessment.
win: Insurers with AI-powered underwriting platforms and data science teams are winning. AIG, Chubb, and Beazley are using algorithmic screening to cherry-pick the lowest-risk clients and price aggressively against their peers. Credit bureaus—Equifax, Experian, TransUnion—control 50–60% of monitoring services and are locking in customers by bundling insurance, breach response, and identity protection into integrated packages they can cross-sell endlessly. Consolidators like Kingswood Capital (which acquired IDX in November 2024) and tech vendors like Aura (now leading on dark-web monitoring speed and depth) are capturing the identity-protection niche by offering full-stack forensics, monitoring, and insurance under one roof. Well-secured enterprises with clean audit trails and strong cybersecurity postures are getting cheaper rates in a bifurcated market; they represent the profitable tail of underwriting.
lose: Mid-market and lower-tier businesses without sophisticated security programs are getting squeezed. Insurers are tightening underwriting, denying policies outright to laggards, or forcing them into the surplus market at triple premiums. Small retailers, healthcare practices, and local governments face a choice: invest millions in security infrastructure to qualify for standard-market rates, or pay punitive premiums or go uninsured. Traditional identity-theft insurers like Norton LifeLock, whose dark-web monitoring (60 pieces) lags competitors like Aura (260 pieces) and whose alert times lag by orders of magnitude (9.2 hours vs. 3 minutes), are losing wallet share to full-stack consolidators. Businesses facing ransomware, third-party liability claims, and identity fraud are bearing more of the cost themselves as insurers narrow coverage and raise deductibles.
worry: The single biggest risk is that claims keep accelerating faster than premiums can catch up, triggering a hard market or a cascade of insolvencies. Ransomware claims reached record highs in H1 2025, third-party liability surged 70 percent in a single year, and synthetic identity fraud is exploding unpredictably. S&P Global predicts 15–20 percent premium increases for 2026, but if claims losses surge 40 percent year-over-year (as they did in 2025), even 20 percent premium hikes won't cover the gap. That sets up either a sudden market hardening (renewals denied, rates spike, small businesses go dark) or a reckoning where one or more carriers blows through loss reserves and fails. Regulatory tightening—California's CCPA audits, the FTC's updated identity rules—is also raising compliance costs and litigation exposure, compounding the margin compression that underwriters are already facing.
one_sentence: Ransomware and synthetic identity fraud are making cyber risk harder to price and easier to deny, bifurcating the market into the protected-and-cheap and the vulnerable-and-priced-out.

title: Protecting the Person: How Breaches Made Personal Identity the New Battleground
dek: As data breaches multiply, the business of checking, verifying, and protecting individual identity has become a sprawling, regulation-heavy industry — profitable but running against the wall.
one_sentence: Background checks, once a simple data-matching business, have become a compliance trap built on hiring volatility and regulatory overreach.
lede: Every hire, every onboarding, every employment verification now requires a background check. But hiring cycles are collapsing, regulations are multiplying, and the old playbook — speed and scale — no longer works. The $3.2 billion background-check industry of 2026 is being remade by layoffs, compliance burden, and AI scrutiny, even as breaches keep coming.
what_changed:
The breach economy has made personal identity a hard asset to verify and a liability to store. Background-check services, once a straightforward data-matching business, have been forced to evolve into compliance experts because hiring has become unpredictable and regulators have turned personal data into a legal minefield.

In 2025 and early 2026, hiring cycles drove everything. Tech layoffs in early 2025 sent demand for background checks into a tailspin — companies that weren't hiring didn't pay for checks. But as hiring thawed mid-year, demand bounced back, making the industry volatile and hard to forecast. That unpredictability kills margin and forces consolidation: First Advantage absorbed Sterling Check in October 2024 and expected to capture $60 to $70 million in synergies by 2025. HireRight and Bchex both moved on ClearChecks in April 2025, fighting for the mid-market. Checkr bought Truework in 2025 to own employment verification end-to-end. Consolidation is the only way to absorb the compliance tax.

That tax is the bigger story. Nearly 40 US states plus 150+ cities now have ban-the-box laws; Texas joined in September 2025, Washington State and Philadelphia tightened their rules in 2026. Fair Chance to Compete for Jobs Act, cannabis screening bans, and a cascade of FCRA litigation — up 30% year-over-year through 2025 — have turned background checks into a minefield of regulatory risk. Every check now requires compliance expertise, not just speed. AI is becoming table-stakes to compete: Checkr and other players now use machine learning to flag inconsistencies and verify identities in real time. But the CFPB's October 2024 circular raised a hard question: does AI-driven adjudication itself violate FCRA, creating liability for vendors? That uncertainty has made vendors less aggressive, not more. Margins compressed; the market shrank 0.1% annually from 2021 to 2026 even as employment volatility exploded. The floor has been hit: there is nowhere left to cut costs without cutting corners on compliance.

The background-check industry is now a proof of concept for what happens when regulation, consolidation, and thin margins collide. What was once a growth business built on data arbitrage is now a defensive hold. Vendors spend money to stay compliant, not to grow. They buy competitors not to expand but to survive the compliance tax. The business of protecting the person has become the business of not getting sued.

win: The Big Three — First Advantage, HireRight, and Checkr — win by consolidation and automation. They have the capital to absorb compliance costs, buy competitors, and deploy AI to flag fraud faster. First Advantage's $60 to $70 million in synergies from the Sterling merger shows that scale and integration matter now more than raw growth. Small vendors and regional players get squeezed out; independent background-check shops can't afford a legal team or the AI infrastructure. Vendors who own adjacent services — employment verification, identity checking, fraud detection — win because they can bundle and cross-sell across a customer base already saturated with regulatory risk.
lose: Hiring has become so unpredictable that mid-market employers and staffing firms are the first to cut; they can't justify a vendor relationship when headcount is volatile. Small business and SMB hiring has slowed, and background-check volume dropped with it. Independent background-check shops and regional vendors are losing deals to consolidated players with compliance lawyers on staff. Consumers lose privacy and due process: ban-the-box laws are meant to protect them, but they force vendors to store more data more securely, which means more vendors touching that data, more data in the system, and higher risk of breach. Regulators have forced the industry to be more careful, but that carefulness is expensive and passed down the chain.
worry: The single biggest risk is that AI-driven background checks will trigger a regulatory backlash that extends beyond FCRA. The CFPB's October 2024 circular already raised questions about algorithmic bias and whether ML adjudication violates fair lending and employment law. If regulators decide that AI-driven background checks are illegal or require human review on every decision, the entire efficiency rationale for the industry collapses. Vendors would have to hire armies of compliance reviewers, margins would vanish, and consolidation would accelerate. The industry is betting that AI adoption is the path forward, but it's walking into regulatory fire.

title: Catching the fraud
dek: When you get breached, a whole forensics-and-detection industry springs into action—and it's growing fast.
lede: Breaches used to be a one-time catastrophe. Now they're a regular business expense, which means fraud detection, forensic investigation, and data recovery have become their own industries. Three things converge: AI-powered fraud is exploding (deepfakes, impersonation), AI-powered detection is racing to catch up, and the legal and financial pressure to investigate every breach has created constant demand.
what_changed:
Three detection and recovery markets are growing in tandem, each addressing a different piece of the breach response.

Fraud detection software is the fastest-growing piece. The market hit $40.4 billion in 2026, with 18–24% annual growth through 2033—up from $18.4 billion in 2022. This is the edge of the battle: companies trying to stop fraud before it happens, not after. The industry has shifted from simple rule-based systems (flag this transaction if X happens) to AI-powered prediction that analyzes billions of data points in milliseconds. The trigger is deepfakes. In 2024, deepfake fraud attempts jumped 1,300%—from about one per month to seven per day. By 2026, 30% of enterprises no longer trust face-biometric-only systems to verify identity. So vendors are layering in behavioral biometrics (how you type, move the mouse, hold the phone), liveness detection (is this a real face or a recording), and multi-modal authentication (face plus voice plus behavior). Meanwhile, 71% of US companies experienced an uptick in AI-powered fraud attempts in 2025, and over 50% of modern fraud now involves AI-generated manipulation. Margins are compressing a little—vendors make 8–12% profit now, up from 5.9% in 2021—because scale lets them amortize R&D across more customers, but wage and tool costs are rising fast.

Digital forensics is the investigation piece, where specialists dig through servers, phones, and cloud logs after a breach to figure out what was stolen and how. This market was $3.74 billion in 2025 and is growing at 15.9% annually. The industry is consolidating: top 5 firms hold 38% of the market. Consolidation is driven by regulatory pressure—GDPR fines exceeded EUR 5.8 billion by early 2025, and 21 US states now have comprehensive privacy laws that all demand proof of what happened—and by the sheer volume of data to investigate. Ransomware and insider threats (which hit 83% of companies in 2024) have exploded the caseload. Forensic firms are moving from reactive (you get hacked, then we investigate) to proactive (we monitor continuously, preserve evidence in real time, and hunt for threats before a breach). AI is changing the work too: machine learning can now detect deepfakes with 92% accuracy and can sift through petabytes of logs in hours. But courts and regulators still demand transparent, defensible evidence, which creates friction—firms can't just feed everything to a black-box AI and call it done. Margins are tight: about 9% profit, with wage pressure pushing costs up. Recent moves signal consolidation: Cellebrite bought ARM virtualization software (Corellium) for $170M in December 2025, then acquired a UAV forensics firm in February 2026. OpenText spent $185M on litigation-workflow software (ADF Solutions). Magnet Forensics integrated with Microsoft Sentinel in February 2026 to automate evidence capture from cloud systems.

Data recovery services are the last-resort piece, for when ransomware or equipment failure destroys data and you have to physically recover it. This market was $5.2 billion in 2025 and grew to $6.04 billion in 2026—16.1% growth. But this market tells a story of economic pain. Ransomware demand has saved the industry: Q1 2025 saw 2,063 victim organizations (double the year before), and 77% of intrusions now include data exfiltration, making recovery a critical part of incident response. Mean recovery costs hit $1.53 million globally (not counting ransom). However, the industry faces brutal structural headwinds. SSDs now comprise 80%+ of enterprise storage (up from 36% in 2020), but SSD recovery is far more complex and risky than old hard-drive recovery—it's also way more expensive. Cloud backup is growing at 19.6% annually (projected $9.25 billion in 2025), so more enterprises can avoid on-premise data loss entirely. And profitability is crushed: consumables (parts, tools, supplies) now eat 50% of gross revenue in 2026, leaving only 50% margin before you pay anyone or run an office. Recovery firms are still fragmented—DriveSavers and Ontrack are the biggest independent players, but Seagate, Western Digital, and Dell all run authorized repair shops—and consolidation is slower here than in software. Still, growth is real: Ontrack raised $50M in Series B funding in 2025 specifically to expand labs and R&D, and it partnered with AWS in 2024 to offer hybrid cloud recovery, signaling a bet that the recovery business will last.

These three markets are woven together. When a company gets breached, fraud-detection tools might spot something odd first. Then forensic investigators move in to gather evidence and understand scope. Then data recovery teams extract files if encryption or deletion is involved. The regulatory clock is ticking through it all—GDPR, CCPA, state privacy laws, PCI-DSS requirements—which makes every step defensible and documented. The result is a tightly coupled industrial supply chain, where each player's growth is the other player's justification.

win: Fraud-detection software vendors are the clear winners. They own the fastest-growing market ($40.4B in 2026, 18–24% growth), and demand is structural—every company needs to catch AI-powered fraud faster than the attackers can launch it. Digital forensics firms win too, especially consolidators like Cellebrite and OpenText, because regulatory pressure (GDPR, CCPA, 21 state privacy laws) makes every breach investigation mandatory and defensible. Data recovery firms benefit from ransomware surge but face margin compression. Cloud backup providers are the long-term winner because they let enterprises avoid recovery needs altogether.
lose: Small and mid-market companies without detection budgets get squeezed. They can't afford AI-powered fraud systems (priced for enterprise), so they rely on older rule-based tools that miss AI-generated attacks. Data recovery shops on the low end get squeezed hardest: 50% of revenue now goes to consumables (parts), leaving almost nothing for profit, which forces consolidation and cuts. Companies using on-premise storage instead of cloud backup face higher recovery costs and longer downtime. Enterprises with legacy payment systems (pre-PCI-DSS compliance) face steeper fines and forensic costs when breached.
worry: The biggest risk is regulatory lag. Deepfakes and AI-powered fraud are evolving faster than detection can adapt. 30% of enterprises already distrust face-biometric systems, and 50% of fraud now uses AI manipulation. But courts and regulators are still catching up to what "defensible evidence" means in an AI-powered world. A black-box fraud-detection model might catch 95% of attacks, but if a court rejects it as untransparent, the whole system breaks. Also, detection vendors are racing to add liveness detection and behavioral biometrics, but these create privacy and user-friction issues that could trigger backlash. If enterprises start rejecting multi-modal auth as too invasive, the arms race stalls.
one_sentence: Fraud detection, digital forensics, and data recovery have become industrial supply chains, each tier growing 15–24% annually to keep pace with AI-powered breaches and the regulatory bills that follow.

title: The Security Software Layer
dek: Biometric and identity detection systems became structural infrastructure, not a luxury feature.
one_sentence: Deepfake attacks and federal mandate spending flooded the market with demand for liveness detection and integrated identity platforms, driving a $12.3 billion industry far beyond its 2021 forecasts.
lede: For decades, biometric technology sat on the edge of business operations—nice to have, but not critical. Then two things happened at once: criminals figured out how to forge faces using AI, and the federal government started writing checks. By 2026, it's now table stakes to detect whether a fingerprint or face on your screen is real or synthetically generated.
what_changed: The US biometrics scan software market hit $12.3 billion in 2026, growing at an 8.95% annual clip—but that number is deceptive. Only five years earlier, industry forecasters predicted it would barely reach $9.8 billion. The jump from forecast to reality tells the real story: demand exploded faster than anyone expected. What changed was the nature of the threat. Between January and August 2025 alone, one financial institution blocked 8,065 biometric injection-attack attempts using AI-generated deepfakes. In the first quarter of 2025, Sumsub documented a 1,100% surge in deepfake fraud and a 311% rise in fake identity documents—the kind of numbers that make executives stop arguing about ROI and start signing checks. This forced a complete rethinking of how identity verification works. Banks and fintech companies could no longer use a single biometric signal—a fingerprint reader or a facial scan—and trust it was real. Instead, they began consolidating vendors, buying bundled platforms that layer liveness detection (software that confirms the face or fingerprint is actually alive, not a photograph or mask), document verification (confirming that a driver's license isn't forged), and behavioral fraud signals (checking if someone types, moves, or clicks the way they normally do) all in one system. Meanwhile, the federal government was rewriting the playbook for border and immigration operations. The Secure America Act, signed in June 2026, allocated $69.5 billion to the Department of Homeland Security through fiscal 2029, with $673 million specifically earmarked for biometric entry-exit systems and $5.2 billion for real-time facial and fingerprint checks in ICE operations. By September 2026, DHS was required to deploy biometric exit capability at every major land port of entry or lose funding. That's not a suggestion—it's a regulatory trigger. This flooding of federal capital hit an industry composed of 377 companies, but dominated by a handful of global players: NEC, IDEMIA, Thales, HID Global, Entrust, Fujitsu, IBM, and Cisco Duo. The entry of a giant market signal—federal mandate plus fraud epidemic—started consolidating the vendors and the solutions. No single company could build the entire stack, so the winners became platforms that could integrate liveness detection, document verification, and behavioral signals into a unified stack that worked across mobile, web, and physical entry points. On the consumer side, the shift became invisible but total. By 2026, 80% of smartphones shipped with fingerprint technology, and facial recognition, though only 28% of mobile biometric deployments, was growing at 27.1% annually. What had been a luxury feature on premium phones became standard issue.

win: The platform players that bundled liveness detection, document verification, and behavioral analytics won big. Banks and fintechs suddenly needed integrated solutions, not point products, because standing up a fingerprint reader or facial camera alone was too risky. Consolidators like IDEMIA, NEC, and Thales could command premium pricing because they offered coverage across the entire attack surface. Federal spending also created a protected revenue stream—government contracts for border biometrics don't shrink when economic growth slows. Consumer-facing identity verification players that could speak both to banks and fintech also benefited from the shift toward mobile-first authentication, since 80% of phones now shipped with biometric hardware. The deepfake fraud epidemic made these companies indispensable.
lose: Standalone point-solution vendors got squeezed out. If you sold only facial recognition or only liveness detection, you became a module inside someone else's platform rather than the decision-maker. Small regional identity verification startups that hadn't yet built out the full stack found themselves either acquired for a discount or shut out of deals. Banks and fintechs absorbed the rising cost of integrated platforms through higher fees—ID verification that used to cost a dollar or two per transaction started costing more as vendors bundled in better fraud detection and liveness checks. That cost trickles down: fintech customers pay more in friction, businesses processing identity verification face higher operational expenses, and consumers see new identity-verification holds when opening accounts or transferring money. The regulatory mandate also created a compliance floor: every company operating in financial services or handling sensitive ID data had to implement these systems, turning what was once a competitive advantage into a table-stakes cost of doing business.
worry: The biggest risk is that biometric systems are only as good as their training data—and training data for facial recognition and liveness detection is notorious for bias and false positives. A facial recognition system trained primarily on light-skinned faces will fail more often on darker-skinned faces. A liveness detection system trained in one climate may struggle in another. When the entire border security infrastructure or financial system depends on these systems working without error, a systematic bias or adversarial attack (like the deepfake injection attacks already surging in 2025) could lock legitimate people out of critical services or let dangerous people through. The deepfake attacks documented in early 2025 show that adversaries are already winning a few rounds—8,065 injection attacks against a single institution in less than a year means the arms race is real and accelerating. If the sophistication of synthetic faces and forged documents keeps growing faster than liveness-detection technology improves, the entire integrated-platform model starts to fail.

title: Guarding the Physical Door
dek: Physical and digital security converge into one spend as breach economics make every entry point a regulatory requirement.
lede: Every door—to an office, a data center, a warehouse—is now a breach risk. The cost of guarding physical access has merged with the cost of guarding data access. Manufacturers and building operators are being squeezed from two directions: regulators demanding encryption and monitoring, and commodity costs spiking on tariffs and supply shocks.
what_changed:
The physical security hardware market is consolidating fast around digital credentials and biometric access. The electronic access control system market grew from USD 9.96 billion in 2025 to USD 12.65–13.76 billion in 2026, a 7.2% to 8.4% annual climb through 2033. But that top-line growth masks a sharp profit margin squeeze. The top five manufacturers now control 70–80% of the market (2024–2025), locking out smaller vendors. Meanwhile, the juicy new money is in software: biometric access control software alone is projected to grow 15% annually through 2033, reaching $7.8 billion by then. What made this shift urgent? Two things converged. First, regulatory mandates made old card-based systems obsolete. NYDFS cybersecurity rules hit in May 2025. CISA's critical infrastructure reporting final rule landed May 2026. Sweden's new Cybersecurity Act kicked in January 2026. All of them demand encryption, continuous monitoring, and access logs—things a swipe card cannot do. Second, digital standards broke vendor lock-in. Apple Wallet NFC integration went live in February 2026, and Aliro 1.0 standardization released that same month by the Connectivity Standards Alliance. Suddenly you could use your phone to unlock a door, and the data didn't belong to the lock vendor anymore.

At the same time, commodity costs exploded. Steel and aluminum tariffs hit 50% in mid-2025. Baseline global tariffs added another 10% to imports. Polymer supply fractured: 31 force majeure declarations in Q1 2026 alone, with price spikes of 30%. Manufacturers faced a choice: swallow the margin hit or move production closer to customers. Many chose nearshoring. Honeywell's USD 4.95 billion acquisition of Carrier's Global Access Solutions in June 2024 signals consolidation, but also desperation—bigger is the only way to survive tariff walls and scale a cloud-centric software business. ASSA ABLOY, the Swedish giant, keeps acquiring: Kentix GmbH in October 2025 for data center access control, then hit their 400th acquisition milestone in April 2026. Each deal chases either specialized software, regulatory compliance tech, or geographic footprint.

Meanwhile, residential is now eating commercial's lunch. Smart locks jumped from $2.98 billion in 2025 to $3.43 billion in 2026, and residential captured 71% of that volume. Three years ago, the market was commercial-driven. Now homeowners are buying smart locks because their insurance companies are demanding it, or their mortgage lender is requiring it, or they're just done losing keys. That shift forces manufacturers to build two stacks at once: enterprise-grade encryption for data centers and banks, and consumer-friendly interfaces for homes and small offices. It's expensive. Margins are expected to stabilize around 5.9% in 2026 (according to projections from 2022 reports), which is thin for hardware and forces the whole industry toward recurring software revenue.

win: Large manufacturers like Honeywell and ASSA ABLOY win by consolidating the market and pivoting to cloud software and biometric credentials. They have the capital to absorb tariff costs, fund nearshoring, and build the encryption stacks regulators now demand. Smart lock vendors win by tapping the residential boom—insurance companies and mortgage lenders are now pushing adoption, creating a tailwind that commercial markets never had. Cybersecurity software vendors embedded in access control win by riding the 15% annual growth in biometric software.
lose: Mid-market and smaller lock manufacturers get squeezed out—70–80% market share in the hands of five firms leaves almost no room for regional players or legacy card-based vendors. They can't afford the tariff hit, can't fund the cloud transition, and can't meet regulatory compliance. Building operators and enterprise IT teams lose pricing power; they now have to buy into consolidated vendor ecosystems and recurring software fees. Margins are collapsing (expected 5.9% in 2026) so the cost savings that used to come from commodity competition evaporate.
worry: The single biggest risk is that Apple Wallet and Aliro 1.0 standardization (February 2026) promise interoperability but haven't yet proven they work reliably at enterprise scale. If lock vendors can't make NFC mobile credentials as secure and auditable as regulators demand, we're looking at a decade of hybrid systems—some locks taking cards, some NFC, some biometric—all running different encryption standards. That fragmentation makes incident response and forensics a nightmare for enterprises, and it delays the margin recovery manufacturers need. Meanwhile, tariff and supply shocks may not stop at 2026; another round of duties could force a whole category of vendors out of business within 18 months.
one_sentence: Physical and digital security are merging into one regulated, consolidated market where tariffs and software growth rates matter more than hardware innovation.

title: Who Sells the Compliance
dek: Consultants and IT services firms monetize the rising security and compliance burden as cybersecurity skills become a premium, scarce resource.
lede: Every company now needs someone to keep them secure and compliant. They hired consultants. The IT consulting industry hit $821.2 billion in 2026 and captured that demand—but they're caught in a painful squeeze between scarcity of talent, margin collapse from AI automation, and clients increasingly doing the work in-house instead.
what_changed: Cybersecurity and compliance work created a new tier of expensive consulting. In 2026, consultants commanded $300-$500 per hour for AI, cybersecurity, and cloud work—triple the rate for junior and mid-level roles, which fell to $90-$150 and faced compression from AI-assisted coding tools. This pricing power created a vortex: firms like Accenture booked $5.9 billion in generative-AI work in FY2025, and IBM claimed $12.5 billion in gen-AI business, but delivery remained immature. Clients wanted solutions but were skeptical—only 39 percent of organizations in McKinsey's 2025 survey claimed any meaningful business impact from AI consulting, and most saw returns below 5 percent. The abundance of hype masked a scarcity of talent. Tech firms cut 52,000 jobs in Q1 2026 alone—up 40 percent from a year earlier—citing AI productivity gains. Simultaneously, 87 percent of tech leaders reported struggling to find skilled workers. The contradiction was brutal: firms needed fewer junior staff but desperately wanted more specialists. Displaced workers from Big Tech (IBM laid off 15,000+ since September 2024; McKinsey cut 10 percent of its global workforce, an estimated 3,000 to 4,000 jobs, in 2026) were snapped up within weeks by mid-market consulting firms hungry for talent. The consolidation wave accelerated to prove it: 21 IT consulting deals closed in Q1 2026 alone, the strongest quarter in recent history. Capgemini paid $3.3 billion for WNS Holdings in July 2025 to bulk up on AI, data, and process services. IBM closed its $11 billion acquisition of Confluent in December 2025, the largest IT services-adjacent deal, and simultaneously bought Neudesic, Cognitus, Hakkoda, and Txture in the same quarter—all to grab data, cloud, and AI talent. The result was a bifurcated market: large firms with strong brand moats and existing compliance relationships kept pricing power and kept margins thin through sheer volume, while smaller shops could command premium rates on niche expertise but faced constant client pushback on cost and persistent uncertainty about whether the consulting would actually work.

win: Big consulting firms with existing client relationships and enough scale to absorb the talent wars—Accenture, IBM, Capgemini, Deloitte—win because they can promise delivery and have the firepower to acquire missing capabilities. Mid-market and specialized firms win on niche expertise: boutiques with deep cybersecurity, compliance, or cloud chops can command premium rates because they solve specific, urgent problems that generalists can't. Displaced workers from Big Tech win too, absorbed within weeks by firms desperate for skilled hands. The consolidation itself signals that acquisition-driven growth is the survival strategy.
lose: Junior and mid-level consultants lose as AI automation compresses their hourly rates and firms cut staff even as they claim to need talent. The talent paradox deepens the squeeze on them. Large enterprises building internal consulting teams also lose because they now face a binary choice: pay premium rates to external advisors or hire scarce talent and train them from scratch. Clients face the worst squeeze: consulting bills rise as premium skills get scarcer, but most consulting doesn't deliver measurable returns (only 39% see any EBIT impact), yet they can't ignore cybersecurity and compliance demands.
worry: The single biggest risk is that large consulting firms will consolidate so aggressively that client choice collapses and pricing power becomes purely extractive rather than value-based. If three or four mega-firms control most of the compliance and security consulting market, they can raise rates without regard to actual ROI, knowing clients have nowhere else to go. The second risk is that the mismatch between hype and delivery—only 39% of organizations see business impact from AI consulting—triggers a correction where clients cut budgets precisely when compliance and security demands are rising. This creates an opening for pure-play security and compliance specialists, but the consolidation wave suggests the big firms are already buying them to prevent that outcome.
one_sentence: Cybersecurity and compliance work created a premium consulting tier, but the contradiction between job cuts and talent scarcity forced aggressive consolidation and left only the largest firms and the most specialized shops with pricing power.

title: The breach economy
dek: Insecurity spawned a $50+ billion ecosystem — and the winners are insurers, fraud detectors, and forensics firms fighting a war they can't quite win.
lede: Every breach now has a price tag, and every price tag funds someone's business. Insurance, fraud detection software, digital forensics — these aren't side gigs anymore. They're the economic machinery of a data-breach world, and they're growing faster than the original crime itself.
what_changed:
The breach economy has calcified into three interconnected markets, each responding to a single brutal fact: no amount of locks stops every thief, so the cost of being robbed has become a distinct, valuable industry.

Cyber liability insurance swelled to $9.56 billion in North America alone in 2025, growing at 19.3% annually in the US through 2026. Underwriters have learned to be profitable: a combined ratio of 65.4% in 2025 (breakeven is 100%) means the industry is printing money on the gap between premiums collected and claims paid. But the party is ending. Ransomware losses hit historic peaks in H1 2025, driving 90% of all claim severity. Initial ransom demands surged 47% year-over-year. Beazley's loss ratio hit 48.5% in the first half of 2025, a warning signal—when loss ratios climb, margins compress and hard markets arrive. S&P Global forecasts 15-20% premium increases in 2026 as insurers stop cutting rates and start tightening who they'll cover. Well-secured companies with good data hygiene will get cheap insurance. Everyone else gets locked out or hit with triple-cost surplus lines. The market is bifurcating in real time.

Fraud detection software exploded to $40.4 billion in 2026, a trajectory of 18-24% annual growth through 2033. The shift is structural, not cyclical. Deepfake attacks jumped 1,300% from 2023 to 2024—from roughly one per month to seven per day. By 2026, 30% of enterprises stopped trusting face biometrics alone. Over 50% of modern fraud now involves AI-generated manipulation. The old rule-based systems are dead. Vendors now layer liveness detection, behavioral biometrics, and multi-modal authentication into millisecond-speed decision engines analyzing billions of data points. Real-time cloud-based analytics is displacing monolithic platforms. But regulation is a structural headwind: GDPR enforcement hit EUR 1.2 billion in fines in 2025 alone, and PCI-DSS requirements keep tightening. The margin is tight—8-12% in 2026, up from 5.9% in 2021—because every vendor must reinvest heavily in AI/ML and data science to stay ahead of attackers.

Digital forensics has matured into a $3.74 billion market in 2025, growing at 15.9% annually. Every ransomware attack, insider threat, and deepfake impersonation spawns demand for investigation. Insider threats touched 83% of companies in 2024. Regulatory pressure is relentless: GDPR fines exceeded EUR 5.8 billion by early 2025, and 21 US states now have comprehensive privacy laws. The industry is consolidating—Cellebrite acquired Corellium for $170 million in December 2025; OpenText bought ADF Solutions for $185 million; Magnet Forensics integrated with Microsoft Sentinel in February 2026 to automate evidence capture from Azure. The shift is from reactive forensics (investigating after breach) to proactive continuous monitoring and threat hunting. But encryption and privacy rules make access harder, even as cloud adoption and remote work exploded the volume of data to investigate. Margins are tight (approximately 9%) because forensics shops must invest in AI-driven detection—machine learning now detects deepfakes with 92% accuracy—while courts still demand defensible, transparent evidence from humans, not black boxes.

evidence: Finance & Insurance: Cyber liability insurance grew to $9.56 billion in North America in 2025 at 19.3% US annual growth; combined ratio of 65.4% in 2025 signals profitability but rising claims threaten margins.
Technology & Digital: Fraud detection software reached $40.4 billion in 2026 with deepfake attacks jumping 1,300% from 2023-2024 and 50%+ of fraud now AI-powered.
Finance & Insurance: Ransomware drove 90%+ of cyber insurance claim severity in H1 2025; Beazley's loss ratio hit 48.5%, prompting S&P to forecast 15-20% premium increases for 2026.
Technology & Digital: Digital forensics grew to $3.74 billion in 2025 at 15.9% annual growth, with 30% of enterprises no longer trusting face biometrics alone by 2026.
Regulation: GDPR enforcement hit EUR 1.2 billion in fines in 2025; CCPA audits mandate took effect January 2026; 21 US states now have comprehensive privacy laws driving compliance demand.
win: Insurers, fraud-detection vendors, and forensics firms. They've built a recession-resistant machine: every business that gets hit now pays into it (insurance premiums), and every business afraid of getting hit buys AI-powered detection software. Consolidation in forensics (Cellebrite, OpenText, Magnet) is concentrating profits. Insurers like Chubb and Beazley are printing 65%+ combined ratios despite record claims. Fraud-detection vendors are scaling from 5.9% margins in 2021 to 8-12% in 2026 as they move upmarket and automate. The ecosystem feeds itself.
lose: Small businesses and underfunded IT teams. Insurance is bifurcating: if your security posture is weak, you'll face denial, exclusions, or 3x-cost surplus lines. Mid-market companies without dedicated security budgets will see cyber insurance become unaffordable in the 2026 hard market. Technology vendors without AI/ML investment (the 160 smaller fraud-detection players outside the top 50) face extinction as customers consolidate onto platforms that detect 92% of deepfakes and analyze billions of data points in milliseconds. Smaller forensics shops can't afford the consolidation play—Cellebrite and OpenText are buying out competition—and courts now expect AI-augmented investigation, not manual labor.
worry: The biggest risk is that this economy insures failure instead of preventing it. Insurers are profitable precisely because they write premiums faster than claims exceed them—but ransomware claims are accelerating, deepfake attacks jumped 1,300% in one year, and AI-powered fraud is scaling faster than detection can scale. If claim losses rise 40% year-over-year while competitive pressure keeps premiums flat, the 65.4% combined ratio becomes a 100%+ underwater ratio and the market hardens violently: denial for mid-market, 2-3x price spikes for everyone else, and a cascade of uninsured or uninsurable businesses. The breach economy is profitable only as long as it's treating symptoms, not the disease. If the disease gets worse faster than insurance can price it, the whole system breaks.
one_sentence: The cost of insecurity—insurance, fraud detection, forensics—has become a $50+ billion industry, profitable only if breach rates stay priced-in; accelerating attacks threaten to overwhelm the system's math.
